cards.front: Each partner's side of an interaction is a net: {{c1::benefit minus cost}}, measured against life without the partner.
cards.quote: Each partner's side of an interaction is a net: benefit minus cost, measured against life without the partner.

cards.front: Give the sign pair (effect on each partner) for mutualism, commensalism and parasitism.
cards.back: Mutualism +,+; commensalism +,0; parasitism +,-.
cards.why: Each sign is one partner's net fitness effect, so the pair of nets defines the interaction.
cards.quote: The interaction's sign is the pair of those nets, so it can change when conditions, or the partner's own traits, push a net across zero.

cards.front: Why is the sign of a species interaction an outcome that can shift, rather than a fixed label for the pair?
cards.back: Each sign is a net of benefit minus cost in one environment. When conditions or the partner's own traits change, a net can cross zero and the sign flips.
cards.quote: Scope: fitness (survival and reproduction) in one environment, compared with the same organism without the partner.

cards.front: A host evolves in response to a parasite whose traits stay fixed. Is that coevolution?
cards.back: No. That is adaptation. Coevolution is reciprocal: change in both partners, each in response to the other.
cards.quote: "Reciprocal" means change in both partners; change in one partner while the other stays fixed is adaptation, not coevolution.

cards.front: In a time-shift assay, what does a difference in infection across times show, and what more is needed to claim coevolution?
cards.back: It shows that something changed. Claiming coevolution still needs heritable change measured in both partners.
cards.why: Time-shift shapes are predictions of simple models: evidence, not proof.
cards.quote: A difference across time shows that something changed.

cards.front: When might an arbuscular mycorrhizal fungus be considered parasitic from the plant's side?
cards.back: When the plant's costs exceed its benefits, as can happen when nutrients are plentiful, the fungus might be considered parasitic from the plant's side; calling the pair parasitism also needs the fungus's net to stay positive.
cards.quote: argued that when the plant's costs exceed its benefits, as can happen when nutrients are plentiful, the fungus might be considered parasitic from the plant's side.

cards.front: In nutrient-rich soil, a plant's fitness with an arbuscular mycorrhizal fungus is measured below its fitness without it, and the fungus's own net stays positive. How should the pair be classified?
cards.back: Parasitism (+,-): fungus positive, plant negative.
cards.why: The sign is the pair of nets. A negative plant net alone is not enough; calling the pair parasitism also needs the fungus's net to stay positive.
cards.quote: Calling the whole pair parasitism also needs the fungus's net to stay positive.

cards.front: Predation and parasitism share the same sign pair. What usually sets predation apart?
cards.back: Both are +,-, but predation usually kills the prey outright.
cards.quote: Predation shares the parasite's +,- sign but usually kills the prey outright.

cards.front: Why were Escherichia coli carrying the phage M13 read as a facultative mutualism?
cards.back: M13 infects without killing, and in early tests infected cells grew faster and reached higher density than uninfected cells. The host can live without the phage, so the partnership is facultative.
cards.quote: Escherichia coli carrying the phage M13, a virus that infects without killing its host, grew faster and reached higher density than uninfected cells.

cards.front: After experimental evolution, phage M13 no longer helped the ancestral E. coli strain, even though the infected bacteria evolving alongside it grew fastest. What does this show about classifying an interaction?
cards.back: The same phage's effect differed between ancestral and co-evolved hosts, so the net, and its sign, depends on the host genotype.
cards.why: Rule: a net is measured against life without the partner, and the partner's own traits can push a net across zero.
cards.quote: the phage no longer helped the ancestral strain, even though the infected bacteria evolving alongside it grew fastest.

cards.front: What is a host sanction in a legume-rhizobium mutualism?
cards.back: The host cutting the fitness of partners that do not deliver, such as rhizobia in root nodules that do not fix nitrogen.
cards.quote: A host sanction, the host cutting the fitness of partners that do not deliver, holds back the film's non-fixing rhizobia

cards.front: A legume penalizes non-fixing rhizobia, but the penalty is smaller than what they save by skipping nitrogen fixation. Predict the fate of non-fixers and why.
cards.back: The sanction would fail to hold them back: non-fixers keep a net advantage, so selection would not stop them spreading.
cards.why: A sanction restrains cheaters only if the penalty outweighs what they save by skipping the work.
cards.quote: only if the penalty outweighs what they save by skipping the work.

cards.front: Kiers and colleagues replaced the nitrogen gas around soybean roots or single nodules with argon. What did they find, and what mechanism was shown?
cards.back: Rhizobial reproductive success fell by about 50% in nodules that could not fix. Reduced oxygen supply was implicated as a possible mechanism, not shown to be the cause.
cards.quote: Rhizobial reproductive success fell by about 50% in nodules that could not fix.

cards.front: A study finds that a legume gives fewer resources to a naturally non-fixing rhizobial strain than to a fixing strain, and concludes the plant sanctions non-fixation. What is the flaw?
cards.back: The comparison is confounded: two strains differ at many genes, so the plant could be responding to any of them. Keeping one strain and removing only its service (for example with argon) avoids this.
cards.quote: two strains differ at many genes, so the plant could be responding to any of them.

cards.front: Why does "sanction" in legumes name a measured effect rather than a plant decision, and what can selection maintain?
cards.back: The term covers any mechanism that cuts rhizobial reproduction in non-fixing nodules. Selection can maintain the effect itself: plants that do this leave fewer cheaters in the soil.
cards.quote: plants that cut the reproduction of rhizobia in non-fixing nodules, by whatever mechanism, leave fewer cheaters in the soil

cards.front: Lotus japonicus is grown with fixing and non-fixing rhizobia and given plenty of nitrogen fertilizer. Predict its discrimination, its nodules and the non-fixer's net.
cards.back: In one laboratory study the plants stopped discriminating and made small nodules with fewer rhizobia. On this reading, the non-fixer's net rises relative to a fixer's.
cards.why: With nitrogen in the soil, the rhizobium's service is worth less, so the sanction on non-fixers is lost.
cards.quote: With nitrogen in the soil, the rhizobium's service is worth less to the plant

cards.front: A student writes that legumes cut the reproduction of non-fixing rhizobia by about 50%. What is wrong with the claim?
cards.back: It over-generalizes. The roughly 50% fall belongs to soybean in the Kiers study, not to every legume.
cards.quote: The roughly 50% fall in rhizobial reproduction belongs to soybean in that study, not to every legume.

cards.front: Over many generations in heavily nitrogen-fertilized soil, predict what happens to the frequency of non-fixing rhizobia relative to fixers, and state the rules the prediction rests on.
cards.back: Non-fixers would likely gain ground: hosts no longer discriminate, so the penalty is lost while the saving from skipping fixation remains. This extrapolates from one laboratory study and needs field testing.
cards.why: Rules: sanctions hold back cheaters only if the penalty outweighs their savings; fertilized Lotus stopped discriminating.
cards.quote: the sanction on non-fixers is lost and, on this reading, a non-fixer's net rises relative to a fixer's.

cards.front: What does Janzen's standard require before two species are said to have coevolved?
cards.back: Change in one partner, then a response in the other.
cards.quote: Daniel Janzen's 1980 standard, from his note "When is it coevolution?", asks for change in one partner, then a response in the other.

cards.front: A fruit suits a bird well. Why is that good fit not evidence of coevolution?
cards.back: A fit is easy to explain without reciprocity: the plant may have evolved in response to other dispersers long ago, or the bird may simply use a fruit that was already there.
cards.quote: It is strict because a good fit is easy to explain without coevolution.

cards.front: The cycling in fluctuating selection is usually driven by {{c1::negative frequency-dependent selection}}: a host type does worse the commoner it is.
cards.back: Parasites are adapted to whatever is common.
cards.quote: usually driven by negative frequency-dependent selection
cards.section: Arms races, cycles and the length of the record

cards.front: In a time-shift assay, what infection pattern does an arms race predict, and what does fluctuating selection predict?
cards.back: Arms race: phage infect past hosts best and future hosts worst, a one-way trend. Fluctuating selection: a peak or a dip at or near contemporary hosts, depending on which partner is ahead.
cards.quote: Under fluctuating selection, infection shows a peak or a dip at or near contemporary hosts, depending on which partner is ahead.

cards.front: A lab samples a phage and its host for 20 weeks, and infection falls steadily from past hosts to future ones. Can it conclude that this is an arms race?
cards.back: Not yet. A short record covering one slope of a fluctuating-selection wave also shows a steady fall.
cards.why: Long, densely sampled records with many replicate lines tell the two apart; the cycle length needed is rarely known in advance.
cards.quote: Under fluctuating selection, infection rises and falls with the time gap, and a record that covers only one slope of that wave also shows a steady fall.
cards.section: Arms races, cycles and the length of the record

cards.front: In an invented host-phage time-shift assay, phage infect about 50% of hosts from past and future weeks but only 15% of hosts from their own week, and every time point shows this shape. Arms race or fluctuating selection?
cards.back: Fluctuating selection: the pattern is a dip at contemporary hosts with no one-way trend.
cards.why: Under fluctuating selection infection shows a peak or a dip near contemporary hosts, depending on which partner is ahead; an arms race gives a steady past-to-future fall.
cards.quote: infection shows a peak or a dip at or near contemporary hosts, depending on which partner is ahead.

cards.front: Must a host-parasite arms race continue indefinitely?
cards.back: No. Escalation can slow or stop.
cards.quote: Arms races need not run forever: escalation can slow or stop.
cards.section: Arms races, cycles and the length of the record

cards.front: What is resurrection ecology?
cards.back: Reviving dormant stages, such as Daphnia eggs and parasite spores, from dated layers of pond sediment to compare partners from different times.
cards.quote: Decaestecker and colleagues (2007) used dormant Daphnia eggs and parasite spores from dated layers of pond sediment, a method called resurrection ecology.
cards.section: Arms races, cycles and the length of the record

cards.front: What did the Daphnia sediment record show about parasite adaptation and virulence, and what common claim did it challenge?
cards.back: Parasites adapted to their hosts within a few years, and virulence increased through the record. That ran against the claim that parasites evolve toward harmlessness, in one host and one parasite.
cards.quote: Parasites had adapted to their hosts within a few years, and virulence, the harm done to an infected host, increased through the record.
cards.section: Arms races, cycles and the length of the record

cards.front: After myxoma virus was released in Australian rabbits, how did its virulence change?
cards.back: It fell to intermediate levels, not to zero.
cards.quote: after its release around 1950 its virulence fell to intermediate levels, not to zero.
cards.section: Arms races, cycles and the length of the record

cards.front: Phage phi2 evolved either with a coevolving Pseudomonas fluorescens host or with a host held at a constant genotype. What did sequencing show?
cards.back: Faster phage molecular evolution, and more divergence between replicate populations, when the host coevolved. This applies to those laboratory populations.
cards.quote: Sequencing showed faster phage molecular evolution, and more divergence between replicate populations, when the host coevolved.

cards.front: In the time-shift study of Pseudomonas aeruginosa and six lytic phages, how many phages fitted frequency-dependent selection, and how many also showed directional selection?
cards.back: Five of six fitted frequency-dependent selection; two of six also showed directional selection. Real systems mix the two.
cards.quote: five of the six gave patterns consistent with frequency-dependent selection, while two of the six also showed directional selection.

cards.front: In the rotifer-alga chemostats, what trade-off was measured in the algae?
cards.back: Algal clones that resisted grazing were poorer competitors for nutrients.
cards.quote: algal clones that resisted grazing were poorer competitors for nutrients.
cards.section: Rotifers and algae: evolution inside a population cycle

cards.front: In rotifer-alga chemostats, suppose a run started with a single algal clone also gave long cycles with peaks largely out of step. What would that do to the case that prey evolution caused the long cycles?
cards.back: It would undercut it. One-clone algae cannot evolve by selection among clones, so the long lag would need another cause, which could act in multiclonal runs too.
cards.quote: One-clone algae cannot evolve by selection among clones, so the long lag would need another cause
cards.section: Rotifers and algae: evolution inside a population cycle

cards.front: Trace the rotifer-alga feedback loop that repeats the cycle.
cards.back: Grazing favours defended clones; as they spread, edible food falls; rotifers decline; with grazing relaxed, faster-growing undefended clones regain ground; the cycle repeats.
cards.quote: Grazing favours defended clones; as they spread, edible food for rotifers falls; rotifers decline;
cards.section: Rotifers and algae: evolution inside a population cycle

cards.front: The loop is {{c1::eco-evolutionary feedback}}: evolution changes population numbers, and the numbers change selection.
cards.quote: The loop is eco-evolutionary feedback: evolution changes population numbers, and the numbers change selection.
cards.section: Rotifers and algae: evolution inside a population cycle

cards.front: Why do the rotifer-alga chemostat results count as eco-evolutionary feedback but not demonstrated coevolution?
cards.back: Prey evolution was shown, but predator evolution was not tested. Coevolution needs change in both partners.
cards.quote: showing coevolution still needs heritable change measured in both partners

cards.front: Suppose grazing-resistant algal clones paid no competitive cost for nutrients. Predict what happens to the rotifer-alga feedback loop.
cards.back: Hedged: the loop's last step (undefended clones regaining ground when grazing relaxes) relies on the trade-off, so without it that step would be unexplained.
cards.why: The loop rests on the measured trade-off between grazing resistance and competitive ability.
cards.quote: That trade-off closes a loop.
cards.section: Rotifers and algae: evolution inside a population cycle

cards.front: You have frozen samples of a bacterium and its phage taken every two weeks for 20 weeks. Design a test that separates an arms race from fluctuating selection.
cards.back: Revive all 11 time points. Challenge each phage time point against past, same-time and future hosts (e.g. week-10 phage on week-4, 10 and 16 hosts), scoring lysis across several colonies. Arms race: one-way trend; fluctuating: peak or dip near contemporary hosts.
cards.why: To claim coevolution, also show heritable change in both hosts and phage.
cards.quote: For each phage time point, challenge hosts from the past, the same time and the future

cards.front: In a host-phage time-shift design, why add several replicate lines and a constant-host treatment?
cards.back: One line could follow either path by chance. A constant-host treatment, phage evolving on a host held at one genotype, helps tell reciprocal change from phage-only adaptation.
cards.quote: Run several replicate lines, since one line could follow either path by chance.

cards.front: phase lag (cycles) = {{c1::delay between peaks (days) / period (days)}}
cards.quote: phase lag (cycles) = delay between peaks (days) / period (days)
cards.section: Worked problem: reading a phase lag from peak times

cards.front: Invented regular cycles: prey peak on days 12, 52 and 92; predators peak on days 22, 62 and 102. Match each predator peak with the prey peak just before it. What is the phase lag?
cards.back: Period = 52 - 12 = 40 days. Delay = 22 - 12 = 10 days. Lag = 10 / 40 = 0.25 cycle, the classical quarter lag.
cards.quote: In classical models predator peaks trail prey peaks by about a quarter of a cycle
cards.section: Worked problem: reading a phase lag from peak times

cards.front: Invented regular cycles: algae peak on days 5, 45 and 85; rotifers peak on days 25, 65 and 105. Compute the phase lag and say which real chemostat runs it resembles.
cards.back: Period = 40 days; delay = 20 days; lag = 20 / 40 = 0.50 cycle, antiphase. It resembles the long multiclonal (evolving-prey) cycles, mean lag 0.56, not the single-clone runs, mean 0.32.
cards.quote: Run B's 0.50 is antiphase, near the long multiclonal cycles, whose mean lag was 0.56 cycle (range 0.41 to 0.68).
cards.section: Worked problem: reading a phase lag from peak times

cards.front: A predator-prey run shows predator peaks lagging prey peaks by about half a cycle. Does the long lag alone show that the prey evolved? What evidence would?
cards.back: No. A lag alone does not show evolution. The case needs a design contrast with prey that cannot evolve (one clone) and a measured trade-off in the prey, plus tests of the predator before claiming coevolution.
cards.why: Rests on the chemostat logic: causal evidence came from the one-clone versus multiclonal contrast and the measured trade-off.
cards.quote: A long lag alone does not show that algae evolved; the causal case came from that design contrast and from a measured trade-off
cards.section: Rotifers and algae: evolution inside a population cycle

cards.front: An interaction is scored +,0. Why might the partner scored 0 still be experiencing real costs and benefits?
cards.back: A commensal zero is a net: small costs and benefits can cancel.
cards.why: Mathis and Bronstein's 2020 review argued commensalism can persist as a stable outcome, not just a waystation.
cards.quote: A commensal zero is a net, so small costs and benefits can cancel.

cards.front: What do ectomycorrhizal fungi on many forest trees mainly supply to the tree?
cards.back: Mainly nitrogen rather than phosphorus.
cards.quote: Ectomycorrhizal fungi on many forest trees mainly supply nitrogen rather than phosphorus.

cards.front: In Caenorhabditis elegans, a mildly parasitic gut bacterium newly paired with the worm coevolved toward a protective, mutually beneficial partnership when a pathogen was present. Interpret this with the net rule, and say what it does not support.
cards.back: Both partners changed, and the sign shifted from +,- toward +,+ as the setting (a pathogen present) changed the nets. It is a worm result, not evidence for any human probiotic or phage therapy.
cards.why: Rules: the sign is the pair of nets and can cross zero; coevolution means reciprocal change.
cards.quote: That is a worm result, not evidence for any human probiotic or phage therapy.
cards.section: The worm, probiotic and phage-therapy bridge
